client:
I've been really struggling at work lately. Ever since my mom passed away last year, I just can't seem to concentrate like I used to. Some days I'll be in the middle of a task and suddenly get hit with this wave of grief that makes it impossible to focus. 

Honestly, I'm not sure talking about it will help - the pain feels too deep. People keep telling me time will heal it, but that just makes me feel worse because it's been months and I still feel just as lost.
therapist:
I hear how deeply this loss has affected you, both in your work and in your heart. It sounds like the grief comes in waves that feel overwhelming in the moment, and that well-meaning advice about time healing hasn't matched your experience. 

Would you be willing to tell me more about what these waves of grief feel like when they come up at work?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: At work, the grief hits me suddenly when I see something that reminds me of them - an email notification from their favorite restaurant, or hearing someone laugh the way they used to. My chest gets tight and I have to rush to the bathroom to cry, which makes me feel so unprofessional. People at work keep telling me I should be "moving on" by now, which just makes me feel worse about still struggling.
therapist:
I notice you're describing these painful moments with such vivid detail, yet your voice sounds almost brighter than the sadness in your words. That makes me wonder - do you sometimes feel pressure to sound more "okay" than you actually feel, especially at work? 

These reminders of your loved one seem to bring up such raw emotions, and it's completely understandable that they'd affect you deeply. Could you tell me what it's like in those moments when you have to step away to collect yourself?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client:
Yeah, I do try to sound more put together than I feel, especially at work. If I show how much it still hurts, people get uncomfortable or start treating me like I'm fragile. But then when I have to step away to the bathroom to cry, I just feel so alone with it. 

It's been months now, and I worry people think I should be "over it" by this point. The grief just hits me out of nowhere sometimes - I'll see something that reminds me of them or hear a song we used to love, and suddenly I can't breathe.
therapist:
It sounds like you're carrying this grief while also carrying the weight of others' expectations about how you "should" be grieving. That must feel incredibly lonely - like you have to hide your true feelings to make others comfortable. 

When these waves of grief come at work, what do you find most helpful or least helpful in those moments after you've stepped away?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client:
It does feel lonely, like I have to put on this brave face when inside I'm falling apart. What helps least is when coworkers give me that pitying look and say "You're so strong" - it just makes me feel more pressure to keep pretending. 

Sometimes stepping outside for air helps, but then I worry people will think I'm not handling my work, which makes the anxiety worse. I don't know how to balance grieving and functioning normally at my job.
therapist:
You're describing such a painful dilemma - needing space to grieve while fearing judgment from coworkers. That pressure to appear "strong" while feeling anything but must be exhausting to maintain. 

I notice you mentioned stepping outside sometimes helps - would you be open to exploring what makes those moments more helpful than others? We might find some clues about what truly supports you during these difficult times.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client:
I appreciate you noticing how hard it is to keep up appearances at work. When I step outside, I think it helps because no one's watching me - I don't have to pretend to be okay. But I worry if I do it too often, people will notice and think I'm not handling things well. 

The idea of analyzing those moments makes me anxious because what if I can't recreate them when I need to? Like if I figure out exactly why going outside helps, then it might stop working somehow.
therapist:
I hear how protective you feel of these small moments of relief, almost like they're fragile gifts that might disappear if examined too closely. That worry about "ruining" what helps makes complete sense when so much feels uncertain right now. 

Would it feel safer to simply acknowledge that stepping outside gives you breathing room, without needing to analyze why it works? Sometimes just noticing what helps in the moment can be enough.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client:
I guess I can try just noticing it without overthinking why it helps. But part of me still worries that if I don't understand why the fresh air helps, I won't be able to recreate that feeling when I really need it. 

It's like... I'm afraid of depending on something I don't fully understand, because what if it stops working one day? That uncertainty makes me anxious.
therapist:
It sounds like you're caught between wanting to trust these moments of relief and fearing they might disappear if you rely on them too much. That uncertainty about whether something will keep working can feel really unsettling, especially when you're already dealing with so much grief. 

Would it help to think of these small comforts as temporary supports rather than permanent solutions? Like recognizing they help right now without needing them to work the same way forever?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, moderate-paced speech

client:
I get what you're saying about temporary supports, but that actually makes me more anxious. If I let myself rely on something that might not be there later, doesn't that just set me up for more disappointment? It feels like I'm constantly waiting for the other shoe to drop whenever I do find little moments of relief. 

The grief is always there underneath everything, and these small comforts just feel like distractions that don't really change anything long-term.
therapist:
I hear how deeply unsettling it feels to rely on temporary comforts when the grief itself feels so permanent. That fear of being disappointed again when you've already experienced such a profound loss is completely understandable. 

You mentioned these small comforts feel like distractions - I'm curious, what would it look like if you allowed yourself to fully experience them in the moment without judging whether they "should" be helping more?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client:
I guess I never really thought about just letting myself enjoy those small comforts without judging them. But part of me worries that if I do that, I'll just be avoiding the real pain. It feels like I should be suffering more, like anything less would be disrespectful to what I've lost. 

And honestly, even when I try to enjoy little things like a warm cup of tea or a favorite song, my mind immediately goes to "this isn't enough" or "they should be here to enjoy this too." It's like I can't win either way.
therapist:
It sounds like you're carrying this heavy belief that enjoying small comforts somehow means you're not honoring your loss enough. That must create such an impossible bind - where neither grieving fully nor finding moments of relief feels quite right. 

When those thoughts come up about how "they should be here too," what do you imagine your loved one would say about you allowing yourself these small comforts?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client:
I think they'd say it's okay to enjoy little things... but that just makes me feel worse, like I'm putting words in their mouth to make myself feel better. It's like no matter what I imagine them saying, part of me refuses to believe I deserve any comfort at all. 

Sometimes I'll be watching a show we used to watch together, and the guilt hits so hard I have to turn it off. How can I enjoy anything when they're not here to enjoy it too?
therapist:
I hear how much pain comes with even the thought of allowing yourself comfort - it's like your grief has created this rule that you don't deserve to enjoy anything anymore. That must feel so heavy to carry every day. 

When you have to turn off a show you used to watch together, what happens in that moment between feeling the urge to turn it off and actually doing so? I wonder what that experience feels like in your body and mind.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, fast speech

client:
It's like this wave of guilt crashes over me the second I start to enjoy the show. My chest gets tight and I can hear his laugh in my head, and then it just feels wrong to keep watching without him. I know logically that he'd want me to enjoy things, but my body reacts before my mind can catch up. 

Sometimes I try to push through it, but then I just end up feeling worse - like I'm betraying his memory or something. I don't know how to make that feeling stop.
therapist:
It sounds like your body is reacting to these moments with such intensity that it overrides what you know logically to be true. That physical response - the tightness in your chest, hearing his laugh - must make it incredibly hard to stay present with anything enjoyable. 

When you've tried pushing through these feelings before, what specifically made you feel worse in those moments? Was it certain thoughts that came up, or more about how your body was reacting?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech
